problems.title: Two-cell wing box in torsion
problems.setup: The wing box of a solar powered high altitude UAV is idealised as two rectangular cells sharing a middle spar. All walls are 200 mm deep (midline). The front cell is 250 mm wide with top and bottom skins 2.5 mm thick; the rear cell is 500 mm wide with skins 1.25 mm thick. Front and middle spars are 3 mm thick and the rear spar is 2 mm thick. The box carries a torque T = 20 kN·m and G = 27 GPa. Take q₁ (front) and q₂ (rear) positive in the same sense as T; the middle spar carries q₁ − q₂.

parts.ask: Torque balance gives one equation for q₁ and q₂. What supplies the second?
parts.a: Both cells twist at the same rate θ′, since the section rotates as a rigid body in its plane
w: The middle spar carries zero shear flow in pure torsion
Each cell carries half the torque
The shear flows are equal, q₁ = q₂, because the section is closed
sol: T = 2A₁q₁ + 2A₂q₂ with A₁ = 50 000 mm² and A₂ = 100 000 mm²
θ′ = (1/(2A_iG)) ∮ q ds/t for each cell, and the two θ′ are set equal
The shared web enters both cell integrals with q₁ − q₂

parts.ask: Shear flow q₁ in the front cell
sol: Torque: 100 000q₁ + 200 000q₂ = 20×10⁶ gives q₂ = 57.14 and q₁ = 85.71 N/mm

parts.ask: Shear flow q₂ in the rear cell
sol: From q₁ = 1.5q₂ and the torque equation, q₂ = 400/7 = 57.14 N/mm
Middle spar: q₁ − q₂ = 28.57 N/mm, τ = 28.57/3 = 9.5 MPa
Largest wall stress is in the thin rear skins: 57.14/1.25 = 45.7 MPa

parts.ask: Twist rate θ′
Twist: the middle spar is removed, leaving one cell with the same outer walls. New twist rate?
sol: θ′ = q∮ds/t/(2AG) = 9.60×10⁻⁶ rad/mm = 0.550 deg/m
Only about 5% softer: the middle spar is there for bending shear and buckling, and the outer perimeter sets the torsional stiffness

problems.x: In a multi-cell box each cell carries its own constant shear flow, and equal twist rate in every cell closes the problem.

problems.title: Z section floor beam: unsymmetric bending
problems.setup: A cargo lander floor beam is a thin Z section: web h = 200 mm, flanges b = 80 mm, wall t = 4 mm (midline dimensions). The origin is at the centroid (web midpoint), x to the right, y up. The top flange runs from the web towards +x and the bottom flange towards −x. A sagging moment M = 5 kN·m acts about the horizontal x axis (top in compression for a symmetric section), with zero moment about y. For this sign convention σ = M(I_xy x − I_y y)/(I_x I_y − I_xy²). Thin-wall approximations apply: I_x = 9.067×10⁶ mm⁴ and I_y = 1.365×10⁶ mm⁴.

parts.ask: Product of area I_xy, in units of 10⁶ mm⁴
sol: Top flange: t·(b²/2)·(h/2); bottom flange: t·(−b²/2)·(−h/2); both positive

parts.ask: Bending stress at the web to top flange corner (x = 0, y = 100 mm)
sol: The symmetric formula My/I_x would give only −55.1 MPa

parts.ask: Bending stress at the tip of the top flange (x = 80 mm, y = 100 mm)
sol: σ = +58.6 MPa: tension at the top of a sagging beam, because the neutral axis is steeply tilted

parts.ask: Where is the neutral axis?
parts.a: Through the centroid at 61.9° above the +x axis
w: Along the x axis, as for any section under a moment about x
Through the centroid at 28.1° above the +x axis
Through the centroid at 61.9° below the +x axis
sol: σ = 0 gives I_xy x = I_y y, so y/x = I_xy/I_y = 1.875
Angle = atan(1.875) = 61.9°; the beam also deflects sideways

parts.ask: Twist: the top flange is bonded to a stiff floor panel that allows only vertical deflection. Stress at the same corner (0, 100 mm)?
sol: Curvature is now forced into the vertical plane, so σ = −E κ y
The panel supplies the lateral moment needed; σ = −M y/I_x = −5e6·100/9.067e6 = −55.1 MPa
This is why Z stringers behave well once attached to a skin

problems.x: A Z section has a nonzero product of area, so a moment about one axis tilts the neutral axis and drives the peak stress to the web corners.

problems.title: Launch pad crane hook: Winkler versus straight beam
problems.setup: A crane hook on a launch pad gantry has a rectangular critical section 30 mm thick and 60 mm deep in the radial direction, with inner radius r_i = 40 mm and outer radius r_o = 100 mm about the centre of curvature O. It lifts P = 20 kN whose line of action passes through O. At the critical section (horizontal through O) the section carries a tension P and a moment M = P r̄, where r̄ = 70 mm is the centroidal radius. Use σ = P/A + M(r_n − r)/(A e r) with e = r̄ − r_n (tension positive).

parts.ask: Radius of the neutral axis r_n
sol: Rectangle: r_n = h/ln(r_o/r_i) = 60/ln(2.5)
r_n = 65.48 mm, so e = 70 − 65.48 = 4.52 mm, shifted towards O

parts.ask: Total stress at the inner fibre (r = 40 mm)
sol: σ_i = 11.1 + 109.6 = 120.8 MPa tension

parts.ask: Total stress at the outer fibre (r = 100 mm)
sol: σ_o = 11.1 − 59.4 = −48.3 MPa compression

parts.ask: Inner fibre stress from the straight beam formula P/A + Mc/I
sol: Winkler is 36% higher at the inner fibre: r̄/h = 1.17 is a sharply curved beam

parts.ask: Real hooks use a trapezoidal section, wide at the inner edge. Why?
parts.a: Material at the inner edge pulls the neutral axis inward and lowers the peak inner tension, balancing the two fibre stresses
w: It raises the centroidal radius so the moment arm grows
It moves material outward to carry the larger outer compression
It makes the stress distribution linear so the straight beam formula applies
sol: Fibres near O are short, so a given rotation strains them more: the stress is hyperbolic and peaks inside
Widening the inner side adds area where stress is highest and evens out σ_i and σ_o

problems.x: In a sharply curved beam the neutral axis shifts towards the centre of curvature and the inner fibre carries the peak stress.

problems.title: Semicircular habitat rib: two-hinged arch by Castigliano
problems.setup: A steel rib for a Mars surface shelter is a semicircular arch of radius R = 3 m, pinned at both feet on the same level. A point load P = 30 kN hangs from the crown. Use bending energy only, U = ∫M² R dφ/(2EI), with φ measured at the centre O from the radius to the left foot. Take the horizontal thrust H at each foot (acting inward) as the redundant. M is positive when the inner face is in tension.

parts.ask: How do you find H?
parts.a: One redundant: set ∂U/∂H = 0, since the pinned feet allow zero relative spread
w: Statically determinate: H = P/2 from moment equilibrium about a foot
Two redundants: H and the crown moment, from ∂U/∂H = 0 and ∂U/∂M = 0
Set ∂U/∂P = 0 since the load point is fixed
sol: Four reaction components, three equilibrium equations: one redundant
Castigliano: the spread of the feet ∂U/∂H equals zero

parts.ask: Horizontal thrust H
sol: Left half: M(φ) = (P/2)R(1 − cos φ) − H R sin φ, by symmetry double it
H = P/π = 9.55 kN

parts.ask: Bending moment at the crown
Largest moment of the opposite sign (outer face in tension): its magnitude
sol: dM/dφ = 0: (P/2) sin φ = H cos φ, tan φ = 2/π, φ = 32.5°

parts.ask: Twist: one foot sits on a roller (H = 0). Crown moment now?
sol: Statically determinate curved beam: M = (P/2)R(1 − cos φ)
Crown: PR/2 = 45 kN·m, 2.75 times the two-hinged value
The thrust is what makes an arch efficient

problems.x: Pinned feet supply a horizontal thrust H = P/π that cuts the crown moment of a semicircular arch to 36% of the free spreading value.

problems.title: Solar UAV spar: one and two term Ritz
problems.setup: A solar UAV wing spar is modelled as a cantilever of length L = 4 m, clamped at the root x = 0, with EI = 50 kN·m² and a uniform lift q = 300 N/m. Deflection w is positive in the load direction. Use Π = ∫(EI/2)(w″)² dx − ∫q w dx. Exact results: tip deflection qL⁴/(8EI) = 192 mm and root moment qL²/2 = 2.4 kN·m.

parts.ask: One term trial w = a₁x²: tip deflection
sol: Π = 2EI a₁² L − q a₁ L³/3
∂Π/∂a₁ = 0: a₁ = qL²/(12EI)
Tip: a₁L² = qL⁴/(12EI) = 300·256/600 000 = 0.128 m, two thirds of exact

parts.ask: Two term trial w = a₁x² + a₂x³: tip deflection
sol: Stiffness: [[4EIL, 6EIL²],[6EIL², 12EIL³]]·[a₁, a₂] = [qL³/3, qL⁴/4]
a₁ = 5qL²/(24EI), a₂ = −qL/(12EI)
Tip = a₁L² + a₂L³ = qL⁴/(8EI) = 192 mm, which matches exact

parts.ask: Two term root bending moment EI w″(0)
sol: EI w″(0) = 2EI a₁ = 5qL²/12 = 2.0 kN·m
Exact is 2.4 kN·m: moments come from second derivatives and converge more slowly than displacements

parts.ask: A classmate proposes w = a₁x + a₂x². What is the verdict?
parts.a: Inadmissible: the x term gives a root slope, violating the essential condition w′(0) = 0
w: Admissible and better, since it has a lower order term
Inadmissible because it fails the natural condition w″(L) = 0
Admissible, because Ritz only needs w(0) = 0
sol: Ritz trial functions must satisfy the essential (kinematic) conditions: w(0) = 0 and w′(0) = 0
Natural conditions at the free tip come out of the minimisation automatically

parts.ask: Twist: a bracing wire adds a tip spring k = 5 kN/m. Keep the two term trial. Tip deflection?
sol: The spring is a natural condition: add ½k w(L)² to Π and keep the same trial
Result: w(L) = 3qL⁴/(8(3EI + kL³)) = 0.0613 m
Check by superposition: 192/(1 + kL³/(3EI)) = 192/3.133 = 61.3 mm

problems.x: Rayleigh-Ritz with admissible trial functions converges first in displacement, and moments need more terms.

problems.title: Mezzanine column restrained by a floor beam
problems.setup: A steel column in a lunar surface hangar has L = 4 m and EI = 2 MN·m². Its base is pinned. Its top is held against sideways motion and is rigidly connected to a floor beam of length L_b = 6 m and EI_b = 4 MN·m² whose far end is pinned, so the top sees a rotational spring k. An axial dead load P acts at the top. Let u = λL with λ² = P/EI and β = kL/EI.

parts.ask: Which characteristic equation gives P_cr?
w: tan u = u
sin u = 0
tan u = −u/β
sol: w = A sin λx + Cx satisfies w(0) = 0 and w″(0) = 0
w(L) = 0 gives C = −A sin u/L; top: EI w″(L) + k w′(L) = 0
−u² sin u + β(u cos u − sin u) = 0, so tan u = βu/(u² + β); β → 0 gives sin u = 0, β → ∞ gives tan u = u

parts.ask: Root u for this column
sol: Solve tan u = 4u/(u² + 4) numerically between π and 4.493

parts.ask: Critical load P_cr
sol: P_cr = 1833 kN, between pinned pinned (1234 kN) and pinned clamped (2524 kN)

parts.ask: Effective length factor K
Twist: the floor beam's far end is clamped instead of pinned. New P_cr?
sol: Solve tan u = βu/(u² + β): u = 3.931
P_cr = 3.931²·2×10⁶/16 = 1932 kN, a 5% gain for a 33% stiffer spring

problems.x: An elastic end restraint places P_cr between the pinned and clamped limits, and a member framing into the joint acts as a rotational spring of 3EI/L or 4EI/L.

problems.title: Guyed mast hinge: the two-thirds power knockdown
problems.setup: A deployable mast is modelled as a rigid bar of length L = 1.5 m pinned at its base, with a horizontal spring k = 40 kN/m at the top that stays horizontal (a guy line idealisation). A vertical dead load P acts at the top. θ is measured from the vertical. The as-built mast leans at θ₀ with the spring unstretched, so Π = ½kL²(sin θ − sin θ₀)² − PL(cos θ₀ − cos θ).

parts.ask: Critical load of the perfect mast (θ₀ = 0)
sol: Π ≈ ½(kL² − PL)θ² for small θ

parts.ask: The perfect post-buckling path is P = kL cos θ. What type is it?
parts.a: Unstable symmetric: P falls as |θ| grows on both sides
w: Stable symmetric: P rises with |θ|
Asymmetric: P falls on one side only
Neutral: P stays at kL for all θ
sol: cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2, so P/P_cr ≈ 1 − θ²/2 on both sides
Unstable symmetric paths are imperfection sensitive

parts.ask: Limit load for θ₀ = 1°
sol: Equilibrium: P = kL cos θ (1 − sin θ₀/sin θ)
dP/dθ = 0 gives sin³θ = sin θ₀, then P_s = kL(1 − sin^(2/3)θ₀)^(3/2)
The asymptotic law 1 − (3/2)θ₀^(2/3) gives 53.9 kN

parts.ask: By the two-thirds power law, by what factor must θ₀ shrink to halve the knockdown 1 − P_s/P_cr?
sol: Halving it needs θ₀ to fall by 2^(3/2) = 2.83

parts.ask: Twist: the top load becomes a follower load that always acts along the bar. What now?
parts.a: The load passes through the pin, so it exerts zero moment and the spring keeps the bar stable; follower loads are nonconservative and need the kinetic method
w: P_cr stays at kL because the energy method still applies
P_cr doubles because the load tilts with the bar
The bar buckles at P = kL/2 by divergence
sol: In general a follower load does path dependent work, so Π is undefined; here it acts along the bar, perpendicular to the tip motion, and does zero work
For one rigid bar its line of action meets the pin: zero overturning moment
With two links (Ziegler column) the kinetic method gives flutter at finite load

problems.x: An unstable symmetric structure loses capacity as the two-thirds power of its imperfection.

problems.title: Garage roof beam on an inclined tie: the cable trap
problems.setup: A rover garage roof beam is simply supported over L = 8 m with EI = 20 MN·m² and a downward uniform load w = 10 kN/m. At midspan a steel cable runs up to an anchor at 30° from the vertical, with axial stiffness EA/L_c = 8 MN/m. The cable is taut with zero force before loading. Neglect beam axial strain; the pinned end takes the horizontal cable component.

parts.ask: Equivalent vertical spring stiffness of the cable at midspan
sol: A vertical drop δ stretches the cable by δ cos 30°
Cable force (EA/L_c)δ cos 30°, vertical part times cos 30° again
k = (EA/L_c) cos²30° = 8·0.75 = 6 MN/m

parts.ask: Vertical cable force R at midspan
sol: Release R: δ₀ = 5wL⁴/(384EI) = 26.67 mm; beam midspan flexibility 1/k_b = L³/(48EI) = 1/(1.875 MN/m)
Compatibility: δ₀ − R/k_b = R/k

parts.ask: Cable tension
sol: Horizontal part R tan 30° = 22.0 kN goes to the pinned end

parts.ask: A rigid midspan prop would take 5wL/8 = 50 kN. How do you read 38.1 kN?
parts.a: The cable and beam act as springs in series at midspan, so the stretch lets the beam take back part of the load
w: The beam is stiffer than the cable, so the cable takes more than 50 kN
The 30° angle reduces the force by cos 30° only
The prop force is independent of support stiffness for a redundant beam
sol: R = δ₀/(1/k_b + 1/k): stiffer cable means R approaches 50 kN
Midspan sag R/k = 6.3 mm

parts.ask: Twist: wind suction gives a net upward load of 4 kN/m. Midspan upward deflection?
sol: A cable can only pull: under uplift it goes slack and carries nothing
The beam is simply supported: δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI) = 5·4000·4096/(384·20×10⁶)
δ = 10.7 mm upward; a two-way spring model gives 2.5 mm because it lets the cable push

problems.x: An inclined member acts as a spring of stiffness (EA/L) cos²θ along the load direction, and a cable supplies that stiffness only while it is in tension.
